entry.title: NPM Under the Hood: How Dependency Management, Lockfiles, Workspaces, Publishing & Security Really Work
entry.summary:
npm install express npm install npm run dev npm publish
But knowing these commands is very different from understanding what NPM is actually doing. When you run: npm install
NPM is not simply downloading some files. It is solving a dependency graph, resolving versions, communicating with a registry, validating package metadata, building an installation tree, generating or updating a lockfile, running lifecycle scripts, and storing packages in a local cache. And when you run: npm publish
you are not simply uploading a folder. You are creating a versioned package artifact that can become a dependency of thousands of other applications. Understanding these internals changes how you think about: package.json package-lock.json semantic versioning dependency conflicts node_modules npm scripts…

entry.title: Making a Mac security monitor hard to silence
entry.summary: A security monitor that can be switched off quietly is worse than none, because it still looks reassuring. This post covers how MacSentry, my open-source Mac monitor, tries to make silencing it noisy: telling a reboot apart from kill -9, two processes that watch each other, an append-only log, a dead man's switch, and a Telegram detail that lets malware delete your alerts if you are not careful. The goal is not to be unstoppable. Someone with root can, given time, stop any local monitor. The goal is that the attempt itself gets reported, from outside the machine, before it succeeds. Anything stored only on the Mac can be cleaned up by whoever gets in. So every finding is sent to Telegram the moment it happens, and the local log is a second copy, not the primary record.
